---
title: Making Your Own Commands
---

Our scripts work, but they do not feel like the commands that came with the
machine. To draw big letters you type `figlet hello`. To print a table you type
`bash table.sh 3`.

Two things are different. You have to say `bash` in front of it. And you have
to be standing in the directory the file is in. Neither is essential, and by
the end of this chapter `table.sh` will be a command like any other.

The `.sh` stays. That one is a convention worth keeping, and it costs nothing:
a listing then tells you at a glance which of your commands are shell scripts.

Nothing about the scripts themselves changes here. This is about where a
command lives and how the system runs it.

In this chapter, we'll learn how to:

* tell the system which program should read a script
* mark a script as one that can be run
* run a script by its path, and see why `./` is needed
* find out where the shell looks for commands
* keep commands of your own in a directory of your own

And the one idea to hold on to from the start: **a command is just a file the
system is allowed to run and the shell knows where to find.**

## Saying which program should read the file

`figlet` needs no `bash` in front of it because the system knows how to run it.
A script has to say so, and it says so on its very first line:

```{.bash filename="table.sh"}
#!/bin/bash
#
# Prints the multiplication table of a number.
#
# USAGE: table.sh 5
#
```

The rest of the file is unchanged. That first line means "read the rest of this
file with `/bin/bash`", and `/bin/bash` is where the shell itself lives on the
machine.

To the shell it is only a comment, because it starts with a `#`. It is the
system that looks at it, before bash is involved at all, when it is deciding
what to do with the file. The two characters `#!` are called a **shebang**, and
the line has to be the first one in the file - not the second, and with nothing
in front of the `#`.

## Permission to run

Now try running the file directly:

```session
$ ./table.sh 3
bash: ./table.sh: Permission denied
```

The file is readable - `cat` has been showing it to us all along - but it is
not marked as something that may be *run*. Every file carries a set of marks
saying who may do what with it, and `ls -l` prints them:

```session
$ ls -l table.sh
-rw-rw-r-- 1 anand anand 247 Sep  9 10:12 table.sh
```

The marks are the letters at the very start: `rw-rw-r--`. They come in three
groups of three - what you may do with the file, what your group may do, and
what everyone else may do. In each group, `r` means it may be read, `w` means
it may be written to, and `x` means it may be run. A `-` means no.

There is no `x` anywhere in that line. Nobody may run this file, including you.
Files do not get that mark by accident, which is a good thing: something that
arrives on your machine cannot be run until you say so.

`chmod` sets it. The name is short for "change mode", and `+x` adds the `x`:

```session
$ chmod +x table.sh
```

```session
$ ls -l table.sh
-rwxrwxr-x 1 anand anand 247 Sep  9 10:12 table.sh
```

Three `x`s where there were none. Nothing else about the file changed - same
size, same contents - and now it may be run:

```session
$ ./table.sh 3
3 x 1 = 3
3 x 2 = 6
3 x 3 = 9
3 x 4 = 12
3 x 5 = 15
3 x 6 = 18
3 x 7 = 21
3 x 8 = 24
3 x 9 = 27
3 x 10 = 30
```

No `bash` in front of it. The first difference is gone.

## Why the ./

You may have wondered about that `./` we had to type. Leave it out and the
shell cannot find the file at all, even though it is right there:

```session
$ table.sh 3
bash: table.sh: command not found
```

The `./` is doing real work. `.` is the name for the directory you are standing
in, so `./table.sh` reads as "the file `table.sh`, here in this directory". It
is a path, and that is the whole point:

- a name with a slash in it is a **path**, and the shell goes straight to it
- a name with no slash in it is a **command name**, and the shell goes looking
  for it

`table.sh` on its own has no slash, so the shell went looking - and it does not
look in the directory you are standing in. It looks through a list of
directories, kept in a variable:

```session
$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games
```

Directories, separated by colons, searched from left to right. `figlet` is
found because `/usr/bin` is on that list, and `which` will tell you where a
command was found:

```session
$ which figlet
/usr/bin/figlet
```

The directory you are standing in is deliberately not on that list. If it were,
then walking into a directory somebody else had prepared and typing `ls` might
run their file rather than the real one. So the shell makes you say plainly
that you mean the file here, and `./` is how you say it.

Being a path, it is not tied to the current directory at all. Go home:

```session
$ cd
```

```session
$ pwd
/home/anand
```

The script is in `scripts`, one level down, and naming that path runs it just
as well:

```session
$ ./scripts/table.sh 3
3 x 1 = 3
3 x 2 = 6
3 x 3 = 9
3 x 4 = 12
3 x 5 = 15
3 x 6 = 18
3 x 7 = 21
3 x 8 = 24
3 x 9 = 27
3 x 10 = 30
```

Read it as "from here, go into `scripts`, and take `table.sh`". The leading
`./` is not even required here - `scripts/table.sh` has a slash in it too, and
means the same thing. People write `./` in front of a file in the current
directory because otherwise there would be no slash at all, and the shell would
go searching instead of looking.

## A directory of your own

A path works from anywhere, but you have to know and type the path. A command
does not ask that of you, and the reason is that it sits in a directory on the
list. So let's put our script on the list.

Do not use `/usr/bin`; that belongs to the system and its package manager. Make
a directory of your own:

```session
$ mkdir ~/bin
```

Then move the script into it:

```session
$ mv ~/scripts/table.sh ~/bin/
```

The name does not change. `table.sh` it was and `table.sh` it stays - the
ending is a note to yourself about what kind of file it is, and it is worth
keeping now that these files are going to live somewhere out of sight.

## Telling the shell where to look

`~/bin` is not on the list yet:

```session
$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games
```

`PATH` is an ordinary environment variable, so we can set it ourselves. But
setting it at the prompt would last only until the terminal closed. To make it
stick, put it in `~/.bashrc` - a file bash reads every time it starts.

```session
$ nano ~/.bashrc
```

Add this at the end:

```{.bash filename="~/.bashrc"}
export PATH=$HOME/bin:$PATH
```

Read the right-hand side from the inside out: our own `bin`, then a colon, then
everything `PATH` already had. Ours is first, so it is searched first. And it
is `export`ed, because a search list that never reached the programs the shell
starts would be no use to anybody.

The file is only read when bash starts, so this shell has not seen it. `source`
runs a file in the shell you are already in, rather than starting a new one:

```session
$ source ~/.bashrc
```

```session
$ echo $PATH
/home/anand/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games
```

Every terminal you open from now on will do that for itself.

::: {.callout-note}
Ubuntu's own setup adds `~/bin` to `PATH` too, but only if the directory
already exists when you log in - and ours did not. You may therefore see it
listed twice from now on. That is harmless, and setting it yourself is worth
doing anyway: it works immediately, and it works the same way on machines that
do not do it for you.
:::

## A command like any other

We are still standing in the home directory, and `table.sh` is not here - it is
in `bin`. Type its name anyway:

```session
$ table.sh 7
7 x 1 = 7
7 x 2 = 14
7 x 3 = 21
7 x 4 = 28
7 x 5 = 35
7 x 6 = 42
7 x 7 = 49
7 x 8 = 56
7 x 9 = 63
7 x 10 = 70
```

No `bash`, no `./`, and no need to be in any particular directory. The shell
found it the way it finds everything else, by looking down the list:

```session
$ which table.sh
/home/anand/bin/table.sh
```

Give `figdate.sh` the same treatment - a shebang on the first line, then:

```session
$ chmod +x ~/scripts/figdate.sh
```

```session
$ mv ~/scripts/figdate.sh ~/bin/
```

and `figdate.sh` joins it.

This is the whole trick, and there is less to it than there seems. A command is
a file. The system will run it if the file says which program should read it
and is marked as runnable, and the shell will find it if it sits in a directory
on `PATH`. Nothing about `figlet` or `date` is different in kind. They were
installed by somebody else, into a directory that was on the list already.

## Summary

| What you write | What it means |
|----------------|---------------|
| `#!/bin/bash` | first line of the file: read the rest of it with `/bin/bash` |
| `ls -l table.sh` | shows the file's marks: `r` read, `w` write, `x` run |
| `chmod +x table.sh` | adds the `x` mark, so the file may be run |
| `./table.sh` | runs `table.sh` in this directory |
| `./scripts/table.sh` | runs `table.sh` inside the `scripts` directory |
| a name with a slash | a path - the shell goes straight there |
| a name with no slash | a command name - the shell searches `PATH` for it |
| `$PATH` | the directories the shell searches for a command, in order |
| `which figlet` | shows which file the shell would run for that name |
| `~/bin` | the customary place for commands of your own |
| `export PATH=$HOME/bin:$PATH` | adds `~/bin` to the front of the search list |
| `~/.bashrc` | read by bash every time it starts; put the line here to keep it |
| `source ~/.bashrc` | reads the file into the shell you are in, without opening a new one |

And the one idea to carry forward: a command is nothing more than a file the
system is allowed to run and the shell knows where to find.
